blocks.text: a dog also hears what we do not say
The power of emotions in speech

Our dog observes us on all sensory levels. It learns quite quickly to recognise from our speech how we feel and what the consequences are for it. It converts these insights into its own reaction or defence patterns, which are optimal for it. These reaction patterns do not match our expectations as long as we cannot control our emotions.

In the section “Body language” we learned that dogs study and interpret our body language very precisely. In connection with verbal communication, we should become completely clear that our body language is directly and inseparably linked to our way of communicating verbally.

The relationship between thinking and what we want to say, emotions and the resulting body language is a complex, dynamic process based on the interaction between cognition, emotion and physical reaction.

Mood, state of mind, perception, presence, concentration and general well-being are essential elements of verbal communication. Our dog observes us on all sensory levels. It learns quite quickly to recognise from our speech how we feel and what the consequences are for it. It converts these insights into its own reaction or defence patterns, which are optimal for it. These reaction patterns do not match our expectations as long as we cannot control our emotions.
Neurology & feedback loops

Thinking and the intention to speak: when we think and want to formulate a statement, a cognitive intention arises in the brain (particularly in the prefrontal cortex). This intention is translated into speech by neural processes. At the same time, the thoughts are often accompanied by emotions, which are processed by the limbic system (e.g. the amygdala). Emotions are registered by our dog instantly.

Influence of emotions: emotions colour our thoughts and the intended statement. For example, joy can make our choice of words more optimistic, while fear leads to more hesitant, panicky or defensive speech. The amygdala and other limbic structures send signals to the autonomic nervous system, which triggers physical reactions such as increased heart rate, cramped movements or sweating, often even before we begin to speak. Our dog often notices this immediately.

Body as precursor: emotional activation influences body language directly. Tense shoulders or a frown signal uncertainty or anger, while open gestures and a smile reflect positive emotions. These signals often arise unconsciously through the activity of the motor cortex and the autonomic nervous system, even before the words are spoken. The body “anticipates” the statement, because emotions are processed faster than verbal formulation.

Feedback loop: there is feedback: body language can strengthen or weaken emotions, which in turn influences the thoughts and the final statement. A calm, composed and self-confident posture increases our own confidence, which makes the choice of words clearer and more definite. As a result, our dog perceives us as reliable and strong in leadership, which of course increases its willingness to reliably demonstrate the behaviours it has learned.
How the dog's brain processes language
A Hungarian study (Andics et al., 2016) used brain scans to investigate how dogs process words and tone of voice. The dogs lay in the scanner voluntarily and relaxed.
The dogs processed the meaning of a word and the tone in which it was spoken in different brain regions. The tone of voice was processed in a similar way to humans.

The brain's reward system reacted particularly strongly when a praise word was also spoken in a praising tone. A praise word in a neutral tone, or a neutral word in a praising tone, triggered this reaction significantly more weakly.
For you this means: word and tone of voice must match. The word “Good” said in an annoyed or indifferent voice loses its effect as a reward.
Using clear signal words
Use short, clearly distinguishable words. Signals that sound similar make it harder for the dog to tell them apart.
Assign exactly one behaviour to each word and always use it with the same meaning.
Give a signal only once. If it is repeated several times, the dog learns that it does not have to react immediately.
Together with everyone who works with the dog, agree on a uniform list of words. Different words for the same behaviour lead to misunderstandings.
Only build up a new word once the response to the known words is reliable. The dog links the word to the behaviour through many repetitions in simple situations.
Using tone of voice to suit the situation

Speak in a lively and warm way when praising, and quietly and evenly in calm situations. This corresponds to your principle from the “Motivation” block: calm motivation for calm situations and intense motivation for letting loose.
Call your dog with an inviting, clear voice. A threatening or impatient tone can cause the dog to hesitate or keep its distance.
For instructions, use a calm, firm voice without volume. A loud signal increases arousal and makes concentration harder.
Keep your speaking pace even and leave pauses between the signals so that the dog has time to react.
Exercise: recording your own voice
During a training session, record three to five minutes of audio with your smartphone.
Listen to the recording calmly. Pay attention to volume, pitch, speaking pace and the number of repetitions of a signal.
For every praise word, check whether the tone matches the word, and for every signal, whether you gave it only once.
Record your observations under “My reflection” at the end of this page and choose one point that you will change deliberately in the following week.
For this, feel free to use our Android app HundeWildnis with the tools 'Speech Trainer' and 'Volume Trainer'

Practice: control the speaker within you

Before you speak to the dog, pause briefly and smile inwardly. Make sure that the pitch of your voice falls slightly at the end of the word instead of rising. Observe whether and how, over time, your dog finds its way more quickly into a positive reaction and relaxation through this calm, deep resonance.
Positive consequences of observing this

Positive verbal communication is an indispensable basis for understanding between human and dog, free of misunderstandings. The risk of misinformation is minimised and an essential stress component is thereby eliminated. Living with the dog becomes harmonious and relaxed, which in turn has a strongly positive influence on the dog's leadability and reliability. In humans, positive verbal communication leads to relaxation and, as a result, to a calm and fair way of treating the dog. Studies have allowed conclusions to be drawn about the connection between voice and state of mind (Handlin et al. (2011))
Negative consequences of not observing this

Poor, negative verbal communication (harsh tone, shouting, an annoyed or threatening voice) towards the dog in everyday life and training often leads to stress, insecurity and fear, as a result of which the dog cooperates less, learns worse, makes mistakes more often, seeks distance or even reacts with appeasement signals and avoidance behaviour. At the same time the bond with the human suffers, trust decreases and in the long term behaviour problems such as anxiety, reactivity or passivity can arise.

Positive verbal communication from the human to the dog is another important basis for a stable relationship. It creates relaxing, positive energies in the dog, lowers stress, and clearly promotes willingness to learn and cooperation. Positive verbal communication increases attention and releases oxytocin (bonding hormone) in dog and human. In the long term, this creates a deep, trusting bond that makes our training more effective, prevents behaviour problems and leads to a more harmonious everyday life for human and dog.
